variants.name: Mutable accumulator parameter (StringBuilder / Collection<T>)
variants.idiom_name: StringBuilder / Collection<T> parameter (java.lang.Appendable as the narrow type)
variants.implementation_notes: Collecting is done with a mutable parameter: methods take `StringBuilder` (or the narrower `Appendable`) for text or `Collection<T>`/`List<T>` for objects and call `append`/`add`, while the caller owns the accumulator. Naming the parameter as the interface actually needed - `Appendable`, `Collection` - keeps producers independent of the concrete accumulator, and `StringBuilder` arrived in Java 5 alongside the enhanced for loop that drives most such walks. Where the producers are pipeline stages in a stream, the `Collector` variant is the functional sibling.
pitfalls: `StringBuilder` is not safe for use by multiple threads (the Javadoc points at `StringBuffer` for that case), and `ArrayList` tolerates no concurrent writes: parallel producers need per-producer accumulators plus a merge.
Passing a `StringBuilder` invites callees to build formatting chains (`sb.append(a).append(b)`), mixing presentation into producers that should only contribute.
A `Collection<T>` parameter exposes the caller's container: use the narrowest interface and never let producers read, sort or clear it.

variants.name: Collector handed to a stream pipeline (mutable reduction)
variants.implementation_notes: Instead of threading a mutable parameter through methods, hand the accumulator contract to the stream pipeline: a `Collector` bundles supplier, accumulator, combiner and finisher (`Collectors.toList`, `toCollection`, `joining`, `groupingBy`), and `stream.collect(supplier, accumulator, combiner)` spells the same mutable reduction out inline. This is the right form when the producers are pipeline stages and can be partitioned - the framework creates one container per partition and merges them, which a single shared collecting parameter cannot do. Keep the classic parameter form when the producers are a call tree rather than a stream.
pitfalls: Collector contracts are enforced at run time: reusing a container across accumulator/combiner phases, or mutating a finished result, is undefined behaviour.
`Collectors.toList()` promises nothing about type, mutability or ordering; ask for `toCollection(ArrayList::new)` when the concrete type matters.
A non-concurrent collector with a shared accumulator breaks under `parallelStream()`: keep containers thread-confined unless the collector declares CONCURRENT.
